source_batch.unit_label: ABFM Module B unit 1 (courseware unit 7): sources of finance and financial strategies

facts.statement: Why finance and financial strategies (courseware): finance is needed to establish and to run businesses; long-term finance comes from owners or promoters (their money stays in the project) and from long-term borrowing when the project is too big; bridge finance is temporary funding for the gap before long-term loans are released; the debt equity ratio says how much promoters contribute as equity and how much they borrow, and a general and safe norm is that for Rs 100 of equity one can safely borrow up to Rs 200. Working capital finance depends on the gap between current assets and current liabilities, which a bank finances after the borrower brings in its contribution. Financial strategies are the combinations a business uses to meet its funding needs at the lowest cost and the most advantage; clean finance (unsecured, such as equity, preference shares and unsecured debentures) is costly because the lender has no assets to fall back on; the rate a company pays depends on its balance sheet, performance, track record and credit rating.

Equity capital (courseware): capital is the amount invested to establish a business; equity capital is divided into equity shares of equal nominal value; the holder has the right to income (dividend) and to the surplus assets on liquidation, and voting rights (except differential voting rights shares); subscribers are governed by the Memorandum and Articles of Association; shares can be priced at nominal value, premium or discount; shares are marketable and can be pledged; listed shares are liquid. Terms: authorised or nominal capital (the maximum the company may issue), issued capital, subscribed capital, called-up capital, paid-up capital, calls in arrears (called amounts not paid) and forfeited shares. Advantages: no compulsory reward, no repayment, risk capital, a sense of ownership, and more safety for lenders. Drawbacks: a higher expected return and so higher cost of capital than other sources; costly to raise (advertising, brokerage, commission, underwriting, compliance); dividend is paid out of post-tax profit and is not tax deductible whereas loan interest is; and wider ownership dilutes control.

Internal accruals (courseware): the part of profit after tax retained in the company, plus non-cash charges to the profit and loss account (provisions and depreciation); depreciation raises cash but is not a reserve available for dividend or bonus shares; statutory reserves such as dividend equalisation, redemption reserve and similar cannot be freely used until conditions are met; retained profits belong to equity shareholders and become equity on conversion into bonus shares. Advantages: no restriction on use (except as stated), usable for long and short term purposes, no servicing cost, readily available and liquid, and no change in ownership or dilution of control. Disadvantages: a tendency towards indiscriminate application; the real cost is higher because retained profit is undeclared dividend that shareholders expect a return on; over-use deprives shareholders of dividend and may hurt minority shareholders; the company cannot build a dividend track record; the safety cover of retained earnings falls; and funds may be locked in projects less scrutinised than those funded by public issue or borrowing.

Preference capital (courseware): preference shares are preferred over equity for dividend and for repayment on liquidation, but ranked below secured debt; the dividend rate is fixed, like debentures; dividend is payable only if distributable profits exist and is not obligatory, and is paid out of post-tax profit so it is not tax deductible; cumulative preference shares accumulate unpaid dividend to be paid when profits permit; under the Companies Act 2013 companies limited by shares cannot issue non-redeemable preference shares, all must be redeemed within 20 years (infrastructure companies may exceed it), out of profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue (perpetual debt instruments can be issued by banks); holders have limited voting rights, but where dividend has not been paid for two years or more they can vote on all resolutions. Reasons to raise it: long-term funds, cheaper private placement, no compulsion to pay unless cumulative, a known fixed cost, no dilution of the owners' control, it is part of net worth (improving the debt equity ratio) and no security is given. Drawbacks: possible management interference after unpaid dividends, non-deductible dividend, redemption reserves reduce retained earnings, equity holders feel side-lined, prior claim on liquidation, and uncertainty from contingent voting rights.

Term loans (courseware): term loans are repayable over the years as per sanction terms; they are cheaper than equity; period: short term is within a year, medium is 1 to 5 years and long term is 5 to 10 years (housing loans 5 to 30 years); purpose: to acquire tangible assets with long life such as land, buildings and plant; interest is fixed and predetermined by period, risk and creditworthiness, payable monthly, quarterly or embedded in the EMI, and falls as principal is repaid; repayment is by instalments, or a bullet payment, with a moratorium on principal where projects need time; foreign currency loans carry exchange risk and a forward contract may be used to hedge; security is created over the assets financed and sometimes personal assets of promoters; the loan amount follows the asset valuation less a margin, or the debt equity ratio; appraisal examines economic viability and technical feasibility; a working capital term loan (WCTL) is a short-term loan against current assets given when a borrower's working capital account is overdrawn due to temporary liquidity constraints; a conversion clause lets the loan be converted into equity at an agreed price; a moratorium is a grace period for principal. Typical loan covenants: board reconstitution, independent directors, a board seat, lender consent for mergers and large expansion, restrictions on dividends, promoter infusion, quarterly data, credit rating, ceiling on borrowing, inspection, first charge and negative pledge, and maintenance of financial ratios.

Term loan advantages and drawbacks (courseware): advantages: governance improves through conditions; the borrower keeps shareholding and control; long-term loans gain from future growth; repayment over a long period is cheaper in real terms because of inflation; interest is tax deductible; timely data builds discipline; repayment can be fixed to cash flow; lenders are generally considerate in difficulty; cost is lower than equity; and communication with the lender is quicker than with capital market intermediaries. Drawbacks: the real rate may be higher in low inflation; restrictive clauses may hinder a dynamic organisation; companies with heavier borrowings are rated lower; too much debt can lead to a debt trap; and interest is a fixed cost that makes profits fall disproportionately when volume falls.

Debentures (courseware): section 2(30) of the Companies Act 2013 defines debenture to include debenture stock, bonds and any instrument of a company evidencing a debt, whether or not it creates a charge on assets. Features: an instrument promising repayment of a fixed amount at a fixed date; if debentures are issued to more than 500 persons, trustees must be appointed; section 71 covers issue, convertibility, voting rights and redemption; fixed tenure (perpetual bonds are also permitted); fixed rate of interest (zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount); a call option lets the issuer repay early at a fixed price and a put option lets the investor demand redemption early; no voting rights (section 71(2)); convertible debentures give equity and voting rights after conversion. Types: by tenure, by security (secured debentures give a first or second charge), by convertibility (partly or fully convertible), and by negotiability (registered, or bearer debentures which are rare because of money laundering concerns). Advantages: low cost, a known interest liability, a known redemption date, no dilution of ownership or management control, and flexibility. Disadvantages: terms cannot be negotiated after issue, a rating may be required, a debenture redemption reserve and investment must be created, and many investors must be dealt with. Moving from equity to debentures reduces cost, and dilution follows only on conversion.

Alternative financing and private equity (courseware): alternative sources outside banks and NBFCs include crowd funding, peer to peer lending, alternative investment funds, mutual funds, angel investors, venture capital funds, bootstrapping, REITs and InvITs; they serve SMEs, start-ups and real estate. Private equity is the provision of equity capital by financial investors over the medium or long term to non-quoted companies with high growth potential; it is called patient capital and is generally less liquid than listed stock. Stages (Pratt, 1981): seed financing (small sums to develop an idea), start-up financing (product development and initial marketing), first-stage (commercialisation and production), second-stage (working capital for young firms), third-stage (expansion of growing companies) and bridge financing (the last round before an initial public offering). A PIPE deal is a private investment in public equity: publicly traded shares or convertible securities sold privately. A leveraged buyout (LBO) is the purchase of a company by a small group of investors, largely financed by debt; a management buyout (MBO) is an LBO in which the incumbent management is part of the buying group.

payload.title: Why businesses need finance and how strategy is chosen
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Long-term finance** sets up the project: it comes from **promoters' own equity** and, when the project is large, from **long-term borrowing**. **Bridge finance** is a **temporary loan** to cover the gap until long-term loans are released. The **debt equity ratio** says how the two share the burden; the general safe norm in the courseware is **Rs 100 of equity to Rs 200 of debt**.

**Working capital finance** funds the **gap between current assets and current liabilities**, and the bank expects the borrower to bring in its own contribution.

**Financial strategy** means choosing the **mix of sources** that gives the lowest cost and most advantage. **Clean (unsecured) finance** such as equity is the **costliest** because the lender has no assets to rely on.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The rate a company pays depends on its balance sheet, performance, track record of repayment and credit rating.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the lender has no assets to fall back on, so it charges for the risk.

payload.title: Equity capital: features, terms and trade-offs
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Equity shares** are equal-value units; holders get **dividends**, a claim on **surplus assets on liquidation** and **voting rights**.

**Capital terms in order:** **authorised** (the maximum permitted), **issued**, **subscribed**, **called-up** and **paid-up** capital. **Calls in arrears** are called amounts not paid; **forfeited shares** are those cancelled for non-payment.

**For:** no compulsory dividend, no repayment, **risk capital**, ownership, lender comfort. **Against:** **highest cost of capital** (holders expect more for the risk), **costly to raise**, dividend is **paid from post-tax profit** (interest on loans is tax deductible) and wider ownership **dilutes control**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Equity gives lenders safety because a higher equity share cushions their loans.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is equity costlier than a loan even though no dividend is compulsory?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Holders expect higher returns for the higher risk, and dividends are paid from post-tax profit with no tax relief.

payload.title: Internal accruals: retained profit and non-cash charges
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Internal accruals** come from **retained profit after tax** plus **non-cash charges** such as depreciation and provisions.

**Advantages:** **no restriction** on use, **no servicing cost**, **readily available**, and **no dilution** of ownership.

**Drawbacks:** the **real cost is higher** because retained profit is **undeclared dividend**; shareholders (especially minority holders) lose **dividends**; the company cannot build a **dividend track record**; and money may go into **less scrutinised** projects. **Depreciation** adds cash but is **not a reserve** to pay dividends or issue bonus shares.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Retained earnings can become equity when converted into bonus shares, where regulations permit.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is retained profit not free?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It belongs to equity shareholders, who expect a return on it, so it carries an opportunity cost.

payload.title: Preference shares: a quasi-risk capital
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Preference shares** rank **ahead of equity** for dividend and for repayment on liquidation, but **behind secured debt**. The **dividend is fixed**, **not compulsory** unless the shares are **cumulative**, and paid from **post-tax profit** (not tax deductible).

Under the courseware's account of the Companies Act 2013 they must be **redeemable within 20 years** (infrastructure companies can exceed this). Holders have **limited voting rights**, but if dividend is unpaid for **two years or more** they can **vote on all resolutions**.

**Why raise it:** long-term funds, **no dilution of control**, a **known fixed cost** and it counts in **net worth**. **Drawbacks:** non-deductible dividend, redemption reserves cut retained earnings, and contingent voting rights create uncertainty.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The cumulative feature means unpaid dividends accumulate and are paid in a later year when profits allow.

self_check.prompt_text: When do preference shareholders get full voting rights?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When dividend has not been paid for two years or more.

payload.title: Term loans: terms, security and covenants
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **term loan** finances **long-lived tangible assets** and is repaid over a set period: **short term** is within a year, **medium** is 1 to 5 years and **long** is 5 to 10 years (housing 5 to 30).

**Interest** is fixed in advance and falls as principal is repaid. **Repayment** may be by instalments, EMI or a **bullet**, with a **moratorium** (grace period) on principal. **Foreign currency loans** carry **exchange risk**, which a **forward contract** can hedge. **Security** is a **charge on the assets financed**, sometimes with promoters' personal assets. A **WCTL** is a **short-term loan against current assets** for temporary liquidity strain. A **conversion clause** lets the loan turn into **equity** at an agreed price.

**Covenants** include a **board seat**, consent for mergers or expansion, **dividend limits**, **ratio maintenance**, borrowing ceilings and negative pledge.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Lenders use covenants to protect their interest, which can also improve the borrower's governance.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a moratorium on a term loan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A grace period during which principal repayment does not start, usually until the project earns cash.

payload.title: Term loan trade-offs
payload.core_explanation_md:
**For the borrower:** **control and shareholding are kept**, **interest is tax deductible**, long repayment is **cheaper in real terms** when inflation erodes the rupee, repayment can be **matched to cash flow**, and lenders are usually **considerate in difficulty**.

**Against:** **restrictive clauses** can hinder a dynamic firm, **heavy borrowing** lowers the rating, **too much debt** can become a **debt trap**, and **interest is a fixed cost**, so profits fall faster than sales when volume drops.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In a low-inflation period the real rate of interest can turn out higher than expected.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does fixed interest hurt when volumes fall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest does not fall with volume, so profits fall disproportionately.

payload.title: Debentures: features and types
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **debenture** is an instrument of a company evidencing a **debt**. **Features:** a promise to repay a **fixed amount on a fixed date**; **fixed interest** (**zero-coupon** bonds are issued at a **discount**); **no voting rights**; a **trustee** is needed if issued to **more than 500** persons; **convertible** debentures give equity and votes after conversion; a **call option** lets the **issuer** repay early, a **put option** lets the **investor** demand early redemption.

**Types:** by **tenure**, **security** (first or second charge), **convertibility** and **negotiability** (registered or the rare **bearer** debentures).

**Pros:** low cost, known interest and redemption date, **no dilution**. **Cons:** terms cannot be renegotiated, a **rating** may be needed, and a **redemption reserve** must be created.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Moving from equity to debentures lowers the cost of funds; dilution of control arises only when debentures convert.

self_check.prompt_text: Who holds the call option and who holds the put option on a debenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The issuer holds the call option and the investor holds the put option.

payload.title: Alternative finance and private equity stages
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Alternatives outside banks and NBFCs:** **crowd funding, peer to peer lending, angel investors, venture capital, AIFs, mutual funds, REITs, InvITs** and **bootstrapping**.

**Private equity** is **patient** equity capital in **unlisted** high-growth companies, less liquid than listed stock.

**Stages:** **seed** (an idea), **start-up** (product development), **first stage** (commercialisation), **second stage** (working capital), **third stage** (expansion) and **bridge** (last round before a public offering).

**PIPE:** a private investment in a **listed** company's shares. **LBO:** purchase by a small group, **largely with debt**; **MBO:** an LBO in which **existing management** joins the buyers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Private equity investors seek long-term capital gains rather than regular reimbursement.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between an LBO and an MBO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In an MBO the incumbent management is part of the buying group.

payload.title: After-tax cost of interest versus dividend
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Interest** on a loan is **tax deductible**, so its after-tax cost is **interest rate x (1 - tax rate)**.

**Dividend** is paid from **post-tax profit** and **not deductible**, so a dividend of the same percentage costs the **full percentage**.

Therefore, at the same headline rate, **debt is cheaper than preference or equity** after tax.

common_errors: Applying the tax saving to dividends
Using the tax rate as a percentage without converting

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses that the real cost of equity is higher because dividends get no tax relief.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does a 10 per cent loan cost less than 10 per cent preference dividend?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest is tax deductible while preference dividend is not.

items.title: Why businesses need finance and how strategy is chosen
items.core_explanation_md:
**Long-term finance** sets up the project: it comes from **promoters' own equity** and, when the project is large, from **long-term borrowing**. **Bridge finance** is a **temporary loan** to cover the gap until long-term loans are released. The **debt equity ratio** says how the two share the burden; the general safe norm in the courseware is **Rs 100 of equity to Rs 200 of debt**.

**Working capital finance** funds the **gap between current assets and current liabilities**, and the bank expects the borrower to bring in its own contribution.

**Financial strategy** means choosing the **mix of sources** that gives the lowest cost and most advantage. **Clean (unsecured) finance** such as equity is the **costliest** because the lender has no assets to rely on.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rate a company pays depends on its balance sheet, performance, track record of repayment and credit rating.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the lender has no assets to fall back on, so it charges for the risk.

items.title: Equity capital: features, terms and trade-offs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equity shares** are equal-value units; holders get **dividends**, a claim on **surplus assets on liquidation** and **voting rights**.

**Capital terms in order:** **authorised** (the maximum permitted), **issued**, **subscribed**, **called-up** and **paid-up** capital. **Calls in arrears** are called amounts not paid; **forfeited shares** are those cancelled for non-payment.

**For:** no compulsory dividend, no repayment, **risk capital**, ownership, lender comfort. **Against:** **highest cost of capital** (holders expect more for the risk), **costly to raise**, dividend is **paid from post-tax profit** (interest on loans is tax deductible) and wider ownership **dilutes control**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Equity gives lenders safety because a higher equity share cushions their loans.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is equity costlier than a loan even though no dividend is compulsory?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Holders expect higher returns for the higher risk, and dividends are paid from post-tax profit with no tax relief.

items.title: Internal accruals: retained profit and non-cash charges
items.core_explanation_md:
**Internal accruals** come from **retained profit after tax** plus **non-cash charges** such as depreciation and provisions.

**Advantages:** **no restriction** on use, **no servicing cost**, **readily available**, and **no dilution** of ownership.

**Drawbacks:** the **real cost is higher** because retained profit is **undeclared dividend**; shareholders (especially minority holders) lose **dividends**; the company cannot build a **dividend track record**; and money may go into **less scrutinised** projects. **Depreciation** adds cash but is **not a reserve** to pay dividends or issue bonus shares.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Retained earnings can become equity when converted into bonus shares, where regulations permit.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is retained profit not free?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It belongs to equity shareholders, who expect a return on it, so it carries an opportunity cost.

items.title: Preference shares: a quasi-risk capital
items.core_explanation_md:
**Preference shares** rank **ahead of equity** for dividend and for repayment on liquidation, but **behind secured debt**. The **dividend is fixed**, **not compulsory** unless the shares are **cumulative**, and paid from **post-tax profit** (not tax deductible).

Under the courseware's account of the Companies Act 2013 they must be **redeemable within 20 years** (infrastructure companies can exceed this). Holders have **limited voting rights**, but if dividend is unpaid for **two years or more** they can **vote on all resolutions**.

**Why raise it:** long-term funds, **no dilution of control**, a **known fixed cost** and it counts in **net worth**. **Drawbacks:** non-deductible dividend, redemption reserves cut retained earnings, and contingent voting rights create uncertainty.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The cumulative feature means unpaid dividends accumulate and are paid in a later year when profits allow.

self_check.prompt_text: When do preference shareholders get full voting rights?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When dividend has not been paid for two years or more.

items.title: Term loans: terms, security and covenants
items.core_explanation_md:
A **term loan** finances **long-lived tangible assets** and is repaid over a set period: **short term** is within a year, **medium** is 1 to 5 years and **long** is 5 to 10 years (housing 5 to 30).

**Interest** is fixed in advance and falls as principal is repaid. **Repayment** may be by instalments, EMI or a **bullet**, with a **moratorium** (grace period) on principal. **Foreign currency loans** carry **exchange risk**, which a **forward contract** can hedge. **Security** is a **charge on the assets financed**, sometimes with promoters' personal assets. A **WCTL** is a **short-term loan against current assets** for temporary liquidity strain. A **conversion clause** lets the loan turn into **equity** at an agreed price.

**Covenants** include a **board seat**, consent for mergers or expansion, **dividend limits**, **ratio maintenance**, borrowing ceilings and negative pledge.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Lenders use covenants to protect their interest, which can also improve the borrower's governance.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a moratorium on a term loan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A grace period during which principal repayment does not start, usually until the project earns cash.

items.title: Term loan trade-offs
items.core_explanation_md:
**For the borrower:** **control and shareholding are kept**, **interest is tax deductible**, long repayment is **cheaper in real terms** when inflation erodes the rupee, repayment can be **matched to cash flow**, and lenders are usually **considerate in difficulty**.

**Against:** **restrictive clauses** can hinder a dynamic firm, **heavy borrowing** lowers the rating, **too much debt** can become a **debt trap**, and **interest is a fixed cost**, so profits fall faster than sales when volume drops.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In a low-inflation period the real rate of interest can turn out higher than expected.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does fixed interest hurt when volumes fall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest does not fall with volume, so profits fall disproportionately.

items.title: Debentures: features and types
items.core_explanation_md:
A **debenture** is an instrument of a company evidencing a **debt**. **Features:** a promise to repay a **fixed amount on a fixed date**; **fixed interest** (**zero-coupon** bonds are issued at a **discount**); **no voting rights**; a **trustee** is needed if issued to **more than 500** persons; **convertible** debentures give equity and votes after conversion; a **call option** lets the **issuer** repay early, a **put option** lets the **investor** demand early redemption.

**Types:** by **tenure**, **security** (first or second charge), **convertibility** and **negotiability** (registered or the rare **bearer** debentures).

**Pros:** low cost, known interest and redemption date, **no dilution**. **Cons:** terms cannot be renegotiated, a **rating** may be needed, and a **redemption reserve** must be created.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Moving from equity to debentures lowers the cost of funds; dilution of control arises only when debentures convert.

self_check.prompt_text: Who holds the call option and who holds the put option on a debenture?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The issuer holds the call option and the investor holds the put option.

items.title: Alternative finance and private equity stages
items.core_explanation_md:
**Alternatives outside banks and NBFCs:** **crowd funding, peer to peer lending, angel investors, venture capital, AIFs, mutual funds, REITs, InvITs** and **bootstrapping**.

**Private equity** is **patient** equity capital in **unlisted** high-growth companies, less liquid than listed stock.

**Stages:** **seed** (an idea), **start-up** (product development), **first stage** (commercialisation), **second stage** (working capital), **third stage** (expansion) and **bridge** (last round before a public offering).

**PIPE:** a private investment in a **listed** company's shares. **LBO:** purchase by a small group, **largely with debt**; **MBO:** an LBO in which **existing management** joins the buyers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Private equity investors seek long-term capital gains rather than regular reimbursement.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between an LBO and an MBO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In an MBO the incumbent management is part of the buying group.

items.title: After-tax cost of interest versus dividend
items.core_explanation_md:
**Interest** on a loan is **tax deductible**, so its after-tax cost is **interest rate x (1 - tax rate)**.

**Dividend** is paid from **post-tax profit** and **not deductible**, so a dividend of the same percentage costs the **full percentage**.

Therefore, at the same headline rate, **debt is cheaper than preference or equity** after tax.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Interest is tax deductible while preference dividend is not.
